own_finite_graph_working_proof:
This is a working proof, unreviewed and NOT a caller grant. Let Lambda be a nonzero divisible subgroup of R. It is dense because it contains Q times any nonzero element. Let G be a finite connected metric graph with lengths ell_e in Lambda and positive edge weights w_e (weights1 suffice upstairs). Subdivide self-loops once, using ell_e/2 in Lambda. Define Delta F(v)=sum_e w_e outgoing_slope_e(F,v), and at an interior slope bend use w_e(s_right-s_left). Let theta be a vertex measure with total mass V>0, allowing signed coefficients. Let mu be any nonnegative vertex measure of total mass V. Choose a vertex z and positive rho=V/k times the sum of all k vertex atoms. For epsilon>0 put mu_epsilon=(1-epsilon)mu+epsilon rho; all original vertex masses are positive.

The finite vertex operator for functions affine on each original edge is symmetric, has kernel constants and image the zero-sum vectors: -sum_v F(v) Delta F(v)=sum_edges w_e(F(b)-F(a))^2/ell_e. Connectivity gives its kernel; symmetry and finite-dimensional dimension then give its range. Hence there is a unique F_epsilon with F_epsilon(z)=0 and theta+Delta F_epsilon=mu_epsilon. Matrix inversion on the anchored finite space shows F_epsilon converges uniformly, with every edge slope, to the similarly anchored real solution F for mu. The one-vertex/no-edge case has theta=mu=Vdelta_z and is immediate.

Fix epsilon and a small tolerance eta>0. Approximate the finitely many shared values F_epsilon(v) by g_v in Lambda, keeping g_z=0. Choose the vertex error h so small that 2h/min_e ell_e < eta/2. For an oriented edge a to b, d_e=g_b-g_a lies in Lambda and its chord slope a_e=d_e/ell_e differs from the F_epsilon slope by less than eta/2. Choose rational q1<a_e<q2 with both distances from a_e less than eta/2. The strict bracket also works if a_e is already rational. Insert the point
t_e=(d_e-q2*ell_e)/(q1-q2).
It satisfies 0<t_e<ell_e and belongs to Lambda since Lambda is a Q-vector space. Define G on this edge with value g_a and slope q1 until t_e, then slope q2. The terminal value is g_b. Its new vertex value belongs to Lambda. All original endpoints use the same g_v, so this construction is compatible around every cycle; it does not assume rational slopes on the fixed original edges are dense.

Each outgoing original-vertex slope differs from that of F_epsilon by less than eta. If eta*sum_{e incident v} w_e < mu_epsilon(v)/2 for every original vertex, theta+Delta G has a strictly positive mass at each such vertex. At the sole inserted point of an edge its mass is w_e(q2-q1)>0. Thus the complete curvature measure is positive. Its total mass is V, since Delta G has total zero. The sup error on each edge is at most h+eta*ell_e; choose h and eta tending to zero after epsilon. There is a common integer m clearing all rational slopes, and all values of mG at original and inserted vertices lie in Lambda. Hence mG is integral Lambda-affine on this finite subdivision. The masses at the original vertices tend to those of mu, while the total mass at inserted vertices is bounded by 2eta*sum_e w_e and tends to zero. Consequently theta+Delta G tends weakly to mu, and G tends uniformly to F. This is a finite-graph statement; it has not yet established any actual metric or formal model.

An exact cycle prototype: two parallel edges of lengths1 and sqrt(2), theta=(1,1), V=2, target mu=(2,0), epsilon=1/10 and rho=(1,1). Then F_epsilon(a)=0, F_epsilon(b)=d=(9/10)(2-sqrt(2)). For length1 take q1=52/100,q2=53/100; for length sqrt(2) take q1=37/100,q2=38/100. The displayed t_e belongs to Q+Qsqrt(2) and is interior on each edge (elementary bounds1.4142<sqrt(2)<1.4143 verify both brackets). Raw original masses are189/100 and9/100; the two inserted masses are1/100 each, total2. This illustrates the vertex margin and the bend compensations. It is not an analytic verification.
